approachQuestion.prompt:
A print room receives jobs at time 0. Each job has a positive processing time and a deadline. The room handles one job at a time without interruption, and there is no benefit to leaving it idle. For an order of all jobs, a job's lateness is its finish time minus its deadline; negative values count as early. Return the smallest possible value of the maximum lateness.

Example 1: [(time 3, deadline 4), (time 1, deadline 100), (time 2, deadline 5)] → 0, with the order 3, 2, 1 (finish times 3, 5, and 6; lateness values -1, 0, and -94).
Example 2: [(time 2, deadline 2), (time 1, deadline 1)] → 1; either order has maximum lateness 1.
Example 3: [(time 4, deadline 20)] → -16.
constraints: The input is an unsorted list of n jobs; 1 ≤ n ≤ 100,000.
Each processing time is an integer from 1 to 1,000,000; each deadline is an integer from 0 to 1,000,000,000.
Return one signed integer. Do not modify the input. Completion-time sums fit signed 64-bit integers. Comparisons and arithmetic take O(1).

options.text: Copy the jobs, order them by nondecreasing deadline, then run them in that order while tracking each finish time and the greatest finish-time-minus-deadline value.
options.feedback: For two neighboring jobs scheduled in reverse deadline order, swapping them cannot increase the greater of their lateness values and leaves all other completion times unchanged. Repeating this exchange produces an earliest-deadline order without worsening the objective.

options.text: Copy the jobs, order them by increasing processing time, then run them in that order and measure the maximum lateness.
options.feedback: Short jobs first can postpone a job with an urgent deadline. For jobs (time 3, deadline 3) and (time 1, deadline 100), this order gives maximum lateness 1; doing the deadline-3 job first gives 0.

options.text: Order jobs by increasing deadline minus processing time, then run them in that order.
options.feedback: This key does not account for the time already spent on earlier jobs. For jobs (time 1, deadline 0) and (time 3, deadline 1), this puts the longer job first and gives maximum lateness 4; deadline order gives 3.

options.text: Evaluate every possible job order and return the smallest maximum lateness found.
options.feedback: This exhaustive method can return the optimum, but it evaluates a factorial number of orders instead of using the exchange property to establish one optimal order.

feedback.reason: Focus on what happens when two neighboring jobs appear in the reverse order of their deadlines; a valid exchange must not worsen the objective.
details: Sort a copy of the jobs by nondecreasing deadline, then run them in that order. Track the cumulative finish time; for each job compute finish time minus deadline and keep the greatest value. For a tied deadline, either order gives the same maximum lateness for that tied block.

An adjacent pair scheduled in decreasing deadline order can be swapped without increasing maximum lateness. Repeating removes every inversion. Lateness is finish-deadline, which may be negative; do not silently replace it by nonnegative tardiness.

“Copy the jobs, order them by nondecreasing deadline, then run them in that order while tracking each finish time and the greatest finish-time-minus-deadline value.”: For two neighboring jobs scheduled in reverse deadline order, swapping them cannot increase the greater of their lateness values and leaves all other completion times unchanged. Repeating this exchange produces an earliest-deadline order without worsening the objective.

“Copy the jobs, order them by increasing processing time, then run them in that order and measure the maximum lateness.”: Short jobs first can postpone a job with an urgent deadline. For jobs (time 3, deadline 3) and (time 1, deadline 100), this order gives maximum lateness 1; doing the deadline-3 job first gives 0.

“Order jobs by increasing deadline minus processing time, then run them in that order.”: This key does not account for the time already spent on earlier jobs. For jobs (time 1, deadline 0) and (time 3, deadline 1), this puts the longer job first and gives maximum lateness 4; deadline order gives 3.

“Evaluate every possible job order and return the smallest maximum lateness found.”: This exhaustive method can return the optimum, but it evaluates a factorial number of orders instead of using the exchange property to establish one optimal order.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze the fixed `order-by-deadline` method. It copies the jobs and sorts the copy using stable top-down merge sort with one reusable merge buffer, then scans once to calculate lateness. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Do not count the input or returned scalar as auxiliary space.
constraints: The sort is comparison-based stable merge sort; each comparison and arithmetic operation takes O(1).
The copied jobs and merge buffer are auxiliary storage. The input and returned scalar are excluded.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n log n)

feedback.reason: Sort deadlines once, then track cumulative finish and greatest lateness.
details: The comparison sort dominates and takes O(n log n) worst-case time; the later scan is linear. The copied jobs and reusable merge buffer take O(n) auxiliary space, with constant scan state. Input and output are excluded.
Worst-case comparison sort is stable top-down merge sort on an input copy with a reusable linear merge buffer; input and output are excluded.

methodReveal.title: Compare neighboring jobs by deadline
methodReveal.description: Sort a copy of the jobs by nondecreasing deadline, then run them in that order. Track the cumulative finish time; for each job compute finish time minus deadline and keep the greatest value. For a tied deadline, either order gives the same maximum lateness for that tied block.
